Title: Undirected Graph Inventory
Summary: Build a stable adjacency-list graph and an inventory of components, degrees and cycles without enumerating all routes.
Overview:
Build an inspection tool that turns validated room and tunnel records into a graph. It reports stable adjacency, connected components and whether an undirected cycle exists. The graph representation becomes a shared boundary for BFS, simulation and planning.

Reuse P03's identity rules and canonical undirected edge pairs. Add integer vertex IDs, sorted adjacency and iterative graph traversal. You do not need flow theory yet. A disconnected extra room is useful information; it is not automatically a malformed colony.

Refresher:
A graph has vertices (rooms) and edges (tunnels). An adjacency list stores only actual neighbors, using O(V+E) space for an undirected graph where each edge appears twice. A dense V×V table is unnecessary for sparse colonies.

Names belong at the boundary. Give each room a stable integer index; use that index in arrays for visited flags and parents. For reproducibility across input reorderings, assign IDs after sorting names bytewise, then sort each neighbor list.

type Graph struct {
    Names []string
    Adj [][]int
}
// A room's coordinate is display metadata, not an edge weight.

In an undirected DFS, the edge back to the parent is not a cycle by itself. Detect a visited neighbor that is not the parent. Use an explicit stack to avoid recursion depth depending on hostile file structure. Never enumerate all simple paths merely to find connected components.
Spec:
1. Build an immutable Graph from unique names and canonical links. Revalidate indices and duplicate/self-edge invariants at this public boundary even if P03 normally guarantees them.
  2. Assign integer IDs by sorted names. Store every undirected tunnel exactly once in each endpoint's adjacency list; sort neighbors by the stable IDs.
  3. Report every connected component with names sorted inside it, and components ordered by their smallest name. Include isolated rooms.
  4. Report each vertex's degree and whether any ordinary cycle occurs. A triangle is valid and cyclic. A two-vertex single edge is acyclic.
  5. Do not use coordinates as distances, compare room names numerically or assume input order is a topological order.
  6. Use iterative traversals with O(V+E) work after canonical sorting. Copy mutable input slices if callers might retain them.
  7. The CLI accepts a small JSON graph fixture, prints adjacency lines a: b c, then components=N cyclic=true|false. No pathfinding or ant scheduling yet.

Components.Title: Build canonical adjacency
Components.Goal: Turn names and undirected edges into a reproducible graph.
Before: What is a room's stable ID when input order changes?
Why must an undirected edge create two adjacency entries?
Steps: Sort a copied list of names and build a name-to-ID dictionary.
Validate endpoint identity and edge uniqueness.
Allocate adjacency lists, append both directions and sort each list.
Components.Hint: Canonical ordering is a boundary decision. A later BFS can iterate arrays deterministically without repeatedly sorting names.
Components.Trace: For names c,a,b and edges c-a,a-b, predict IDs a=0,b=1,c=2 and adjacency a:[b,c], b:[a], c:[a].
Components.Gate: Reversing every edge endpoint and permuting input records leaves the inventory bytes unchanged.

Components.Title: Walk disconnected components
Components.Goal: Visit all rooms exactly once without assuming one connected colony.
Before: How will an isolated room enter the work stack?
When is a room marked visited relative to pushing it?
Steps: Scan stable IDs for unvisited seeds.
Traverse each seed's component iteratively and collect its members.
Sort members and retain deterministic component ordering.
Components.Hint: A global visited array belongs to the full inventory, while a local collection belongs to one component. Marking on discovery avoids repeated enqueues or pushes.
Components.Trace: A-b and c alone must produce components [a,b] and [c]. Count visited vertices: exactly three.
Components.Gate: Empty graph, isolated vertices and multiple components all terminate and return complete membership.

Components.Title: Distinguish cycles from parent edges
Components.Goal: Report cyclic structure without rejecting a legitimate graph.
Before: Why is seeing your parent again expected in an undirected graph?
Can a cycle detector replace the parser's self-link checks?
Steps: Store parent information for iterative traversal.
Detect a visited neighbor different from the parent.
Test a line, a triangle and a triangle with a disconnected isolated vertex.
Components.Hint: Do not infer a cycle from E≥V across the whole graph without checking components. Structural tests should identify why the trace closes.
Components.Trace: Trace a-b-c-a. When c observes a, a is already visited and is not c's parent. Compare a-b, where b sees only its parent.
Components.Gate: The detector reports a triangle as cyclic, never spins, and preserves it as valid graph data.

Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run . testdata/graph.json
Verification:
The fixture has a triangle a-b-c-a and isolated z. Expected adjacency is a: b c; b: a c; c: a b; z: followed by no neighbors, then components=2 cyclic=true.

  • A single a-b edge: two degrees of 1, one component, no cycle.
  • A triangle: all degrees 2, one component, cycle true.
  • Triangle plus z: two components; cyclic remains true.
  • Duplicate reversed edge, self-edge or unknown name: error.
  • Permute all names and links repeatedly: exact inventory bytes remain equal.

Exit gate

Explain the two adjacency entries per tunnel, prove each vertex is visited at most once and show why coordinates play no role. Document sorting cost separately from linear traversal cost.
Engineering: Why is a graph representation an API boundary rather than a detail hidden inside BFS?
Which ordering guarantees should Graph provide to all later algorithms?
What would change if the colony allowed parallel tunnels, and why does this assignment prohibit them?
Why is disconnectedness a property to inspect before deciding it is a fatal route failure?
When can a map be useful internally without making output nondeterministic?
What is the tradeoff between revalidating public inputs and trusting the parser?
How does a traversal invariant protect against exponential route enumeration?
